articles.title: The Cure Everyone Stepped Over
articles.dek: For a hundred years, doctors treated ulcers by managing stress and diet — until one man drank the real cause to prove it. Paul says Israel missed something just as simple.
articles.quote: Israel wasn't running too slowly toward God — they were running right past the stone he had already laid down for them to stand on.
articles.body:
On a June morning in 1984, in a small lab in Perth, Australia, a doctor named Barry Marshall picked up a beaker of murky brown liquid, held his nose, and drank it. Inside were millions of live bacteria — the same bacteria he believed were causing peptic ulcers in his patients. No one believed him. Not his colleagues, not the journals that rejected his papers, not the textbooks that had said for a hundred years that ulcers came from stress and stomach acid, full stop. Everyone knew that no bacterium could survive the acid bath of the human stomach. So Marshall did something no research committee would have approved: he became his own experiment.

For decades, ulcer patients had lived on bland diets, antacids, and, in severe cases, surgery to remove part of the stomach. Doctors treated the symptoms because the cause seemed obvious — too much acid, too much worry. It was a condition you managed through discipline and self-control. Any Filipino who has ever been told ulcer yan, sa kaba mo lang yan knows this old wisdom well: ulcers were something stress gave you, something you fixed by calming down and watching what you ate. Nobody thought to look for a simple bacterium quietly living in half the world's stomach linings, because the idea seemed impossible.

Five days after Marshall drank his beaker, he developed nausea, bad breath, and vomiting. A biopsy confirmed it — raging gastritis, caused by the very bacterium he had swallowed, Helicobacter pylori. He treated himself with antibiotics and recovered completely. Two decades later, in 2005, he won the Nobel Prize. Millions of ulcer patients now take a two-week course of pills instead of a lifetime of bland rice and worry. The cure had been there all along, small and unnoticed, while an entire profession built elaborate treatments around it.

Paul tells a strikingly similar story about his own people in Romans 9. The Gentiles, he writes, "who did not pursue righteousness" — who weren't even trying — "have obtained it, a righteousness that is by faith." But Israel, who worked hard at it, who kept the law and offered sacrifices and guarded the Sabbath, "have not attained their goal." Why not? Paul doesn't say they were insincere. He says exactly where they tripped.

"Why not? Because they pursued it not by faith but as if it were by works. They stumbled over the stumbling stone. As it is written: 'See, I lay in Zion a stone that causes people to stumble and a rock that makes them fall, and the one who believes in him will never be put to shame.'" (Romans 9:32–33, NIV)

Notice what's happening here. Israel wasn't lazy. Paul says so directly in the next chapter: "I can testify about them that they are zealous for God, but their zeal is not based on knowledge" (Romans 10:2). These were people who cared enormously about being right with God. They just kept reaching for it the way you'd reach for a cure through effort — stricter obedience, more sacrifice, tighter control — while the actual answer sat in plain view, a stone already laid down, not to climb over, but to stand on.

It's worth asking why a stone meant to hold people up became, instead, something they fell over. The answer is almost the same as Marshall's story: they were looking for something complicated, so they missed something simple. A cure you have to earn feels more dignified than a cure you're simply given. A religion of effort makes sense to us; grace, oddly, does not. So when God laid the stone — the Messiah, the finished work of Christ — right in Israel's path, many ran straight past it, still searching for the harder road, the one that would let them say, in the end, I did this myself.

Paul makes the nearness of the real answer almost comically plain a few verses later. Righteousness by faith, he writes, doesn't say, "Who will ascend into heaven?" to bring Christ down, or "who will descend into the deep?" to bring him up from the dead. Why not? Because it's already done.

"But what does it say? 'The word is near you; it is in your mouth and in your heart,' that is, the message concerning faith that we proclaim: if you declare with your mouth, 'Jesus is Lord,' and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved." (Romans 10:8–9, NIV)

Read that again slowly. Not a pilgrimage. Not a ledger of good deeds weighed at the end of your life. A confession and a belief, near enough to be in your mouth and your heart right now, this morning, wherever you're reading this. "Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved" (Romans 10:13). No exam. No probation period. Just the calling.

Here's the turn I hadn't noticed before: the stumbling stone and the near word are the same object, described two ways. To someone still trying to earn their way up, Christ is an obstacle, an offense, a stumbling block, because he insists you can't do it yourself. But to someone who simply believes, that exact same stone becomes solid ground to stand on. It isn't a different gift for different people. It's the same gift — and the only variable is whether you're reaching past it toward something harder, or resting your full weight on it.

If you've spent years low-grade exhausted trying to be good enough — a good enough parent, a good enough Christian, a good enough child of God — this is worth sitting with. The stone was never meant to be hurdled. It was laid down so you could stand on it. Marshall's patients didn't get well by trying harder to manage their diet. They got well the moment someone told them the simple truth and they believed it enough to take the medicine. Paul's whole ache in this passage — "my heart's desire and prayer to God... is that they may be saved" (Romans 10:1) — is that his own people would stop straining upward and simply believe what was already near.

And then Paul does something beautiful with the end of the chapter. If the message is this near, this simple, someone still has to say it out loud.

"How, then, can they call on the one they have not believed in? And how can they believe in the one of whom they have not heard? And how can they hear without someone preaching to them?... How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!" (Romans 10:14–15, NIV)

Barry Marshall had to publish his findings, stand in front of skeptical rooms, and finally drink from that beaker, before the world would believe a simple cure existed. Somebody still has to carry the word to the person who's still trying to earn what's already been given. Maybe that's you today — not because you have all the answers, but because you know where the stone is, and you know it holds.

So here's something small to carry with you. If you're tired from reaching, stop reaching, and just stand. The word is near — in your mouth, in your heart. And if you know someone still climbing, still striving, still convinced the cure must be complicated, go tell them today. It rarely is.

articles.title: The Wall Outside Your Own Door
articles.dek: Nehemiah's building list reads like a boring roll call of names and gates — until you notice exactly where he told each person to work.
articles.quote: Nehemiah didn't hand out assignments by rank or skill. He gave each person the stretch of wall that ran past their own front door — and that's the section nobody had to be begged to finish.
articles.body:
In 1945, Warsaw was rubble. Nazi forces had leveled roughly eighty-five percent of the city before retreating — block by block, street by street, dynamited on purpose. When Polish families began trickling back into the ruins, there was no grand government blueprint waiting for them. There was just a pile of bricks where a home used to be. So people did the only thing that made sense: they started clearing the rubble in front of their own front doors. Neighbors compared old photographs and eighteenth-century cityscape paintings by the Venetian artist Bernardo Bellotto, using his brushstrokes to rebuild window frames and rooflines exactly as they had been. No single crew could have restored a whole capital. But thousands of families, each rebuilding the stretch closest to their own life, eventually raised the entire Old Town back out of the dust. Today UNESCO lists it as a World Heritage Site — not because the buildings are ancient, but because of how they came back.

Twenty-five centuries earlier, a cupbearer in a Persian palace stumbled onto the same wisdom, and it's tucked inside one of the most skimmed-over chapters in the Bible.

Nehemiah had never seen Jerusalem's ruins with his own eyes. He'd only heard about them — from his brother, passing through Susa with bad news. The wall was broken. The gates were burned. Nehemiah sat down and wept, then fasted and prayed for days (Nehemiah 1:4). But he was a cupbearer, a servant whose job was to taste the king's wine and keep his own feelings off his face. Months later, still carrying the grief, he forgot to hide it. "The king said to me, 'Why does your face look so sad... This can be nothing but sadness of heart.' I was very much afraid" (Nehemiah 2:2). It was a dangerous moment — showing sorrow in a Persian court could be read as disloyalty. But Nehemiah answered honestly, made his request, and the king said yes.

Back in Jerusalem, Nehemiah didn't announce anything right away. He rode out at night, alone, to inspect the broken walls by moonlight before he said a word to anyone (Nehemiah 2:12-15). Only then did he gather the leaders and speak plainly: "You see the trouble we are in: Jerusalem lies in ruins, and its gates have been burned with fire. Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem, and we will no longer be in disgrace" (Nehemiah 2:17). He told them what God had already done for him. They answered, "Let us start rebuilding." And they began this good work (Nehemiah 2:18).

Then comes chapter 3 — a long list of names, gates, and repairs that most people flip past on the way to something more exciting. But read it slowly and a pattern jumps out. High priests, goldsmiths, perfume-makers, temple servants, rulers of districts, and — remarkably for that era — a group of women, the daughters of Shallum (Nehemiah 3:12), all get assigned a section. And over and over, the text tells you exactly where:

Above the Horse Gate, the priests made repairs, each in front of his own house. (Nehemiah 3:28)

It isn't a one-off detail. Jedaiah repaired the wall "opposite his house" (3:10). Benjamin and Hasshub made repairs "in front of their house" (3:23). Azariah worked "beside his house" (3:23). Zadok repaired "opposite his house" (3:29). Meshullam worked opposite "his living quarters" (3:30). Nehemiah could have organized the crews by trade, by wealth, by political rank. Instead, again and again, people ended up rebuilding the exact stretch of wall that stood between their own family and the darkness outside. It's worth noticing what that means: the priest wasn't just performing religious duty. He was protecting the ground his own children slept behind.

And notice the one group the text singles out for the opposite reason: "the nobles of Tekoa would not put their shoulders to the work under their supervisors" (Nehemiah 3:5) — even while their own townsmen, listed two verses earlier, worked hard on their section. The nobles had status. What they didn't have, it seems, was anything personal on the line. Skin in the game changes what a person is willing to lift.

This is the fresh angle worth sitting with: Nehemiah's genius wasn't a speech, though the speech mattered. It was the assignment sheet. He gave people the piece of the wall that already belonged to their own life, and diligence followed almost automatically. Nobody had to supervise the priest guarding his own doorway. Ownership did the supervising.

That has a way of landing close to home for anyone who has ever tried to get a barangay cleanup moving, or a family reconciliation started, or a struggling ministry back on its feet. Announcements and assignments from a committee rarely move people the way a personal stake does. Ask someone to fix a wall that has nothing to do with them, and the work stalls. Show them it's the wall in front of their own house, and they'll often finish before you ask twice.

So here's a question worth carrying into today: where is your own stretch of wall — the section that runs closest to your actual life? Maybe it's a relationship that's been crumbling quietly for years. Maybe it's a habit that's left a gap in your own family's defenses. Maybe it's a corner of your church or neighborhood that nobody else can see as clearly as you can, because you're the one who lives right there. Nehemiah didn't ask the priests to fix someone else's ruins first. He let them start with what was, quite literally, in front of their own door.

You don't need Jerusalem's whole wall rebuilt by tonight. You need your own stretch of it — the one opposite your own house. Start there. The rest of the wall has people assigned to it too.

articles.title: The Seven O'Clock Call
articles.dek: A mother who has phoned home at the same hour every night for eleven years shows why God never grows tired of hearing the same prayer twice.
articles.quote: The God who is "abounding in love to all who call" isn't keeping score of how many times the line rings. He's just glad you're still calling.
articles.illustration: OFW mother's daily 7 p.m. call home
articles.body:
Every evening at exactly seven o'clock Philippine time, Marites picks up her phone in a rented room in Riyadh and calls home. She has done this for eleven years, since her youngest was still in diapers. Most nights there is no real news to report — no fever, no school award, no jeepney fare hike to complain about. She calls anyway. "Kumain na ba kayo?" Did you eat yet. "Ingat kayo." Be careful. Five minutes, sometimes less, and then goodnight. Her three children have grown up hearing their mother's voice arrive on schedule, the way the tide arrives — not because anything is wrong, but because that is simply what love does at seven o'clock. Millions of Filipino households know some version of this rhythm: a parent working far from home, a phone that rings at the same hour every day, a family that has learned to set its clock by a voice instead of a face.

Nobody would call those calls dramatic. But ask any of Marites's children what home sounds like, and they will tell you it sounds like a phone ringing at seven — reliable, unremarkable, and somehow the thing that holds everything else together.

David knew that sound too, in a different key. Psalm 86 carries an unusual label in the original Hebrew: it is one of only five psalms in the entire book called simply "a prayer" — not a song for the choir, not a psalm written for the festival calendar, just a raw, unguarded plea, meant to be prayed rather than performed. It opens with a man in real trouble. We're not told exactly what kind — only that it is enough to make him say, "Hear, Lord, and answer me, for I am poor and needy" (Psalm 86:1). The Hebrew word behind "needy" describes someone bent low, worn down, pressed by circumstance. This is not polite liturgical language. It's the language of a man who has nothing left to offer except honesty. He asks God to guard his life because he trusts him (v.2), to have mercy on him (v.3), to bring joy back to a soul weighed down by whatever this is (v.4). And read verse 3 closely: "Have mercy on me, Lord, for I call to you all day long." Not I called once. Not I will call when it gets worse. I call — present tense, repeated, ongoing, like a person dialing a number they need to hear pick up.

You, Lord, are forgiving and good, abounding in love to all who call to you. (Psalm 86:5, NIV)

Notice that word abounding. It doesn't mean God has just enough love to cover a reasonable number of requests before he runs dry. It means overflowing — a supply that never thins out no matter how many times someone draws from it. David could call "all day long" precisely because of what he believed about the one he was calling. The love wasn't rationed. It didn't wear thin the way our own patience wears thin after the third phone call about the same worry. It was abounding — and abounding to all who call, not just the ones who call rarely, or eloquently, or only when the emergency is large enough to justify the interruption.

It's worth asking why we sometimes feel embarrassed to bring the same worry to God twice in one day, as though repetition is proof we didn't really believe the first answer. But look again at who is praying here. This is David — a king, a warrior, a man who had already watched God part armies and steady his hand in battle. And even he calls "all day long," because a few verses later he tells us exactly why: "When I am in distress, I call to you, because you answer me" (v.7). He isn't calling out of doubt. He's calling out of certainty that the line is open. Marites's children have never once wondered whether their mother's love for them wavers between calls, or grows thin because she has said the same things so many times before. They know the seven o'clock call isn't solving a problem — it's how she stays present to a life she can't physically stand inside. David's repeated calling is that same instinct, pointed toward heaven: not doubt, but nearness kept alive on purpose, one ordinary sentence at a time.

The psalm doesn't stay inward for long, either. By verse 8, David lifts his eyes off his own trouble entirely: "Among the gods there is none like you, Lord; no deeds can compare with yours" (v.8). By verse 9 he pictures every nation on earth eventually coming to bow before God and honor his name. By verse 10 he's declaring, "You are great and do marvelous deeds; you alone are God" (v.10). That's the quiet turn folded inside this psalm — the same man who opened by saying "I am poor and needy" ends up worshiping a God who has no equal anywhere in heaven or on earth. The calling led somewhere. It usually does. A prayer that starts as need has a way of becoming, almost without our noticing, praise.

Maybe you have your own version of the seven o'clock call — the same worry you keep bringing back to God, the same name you keep lifting up, the same ache that hasn't resolved on the schedule you were hoping for. Psalm 86 says you don't owe anyone an apology for that. You don't need a new prayer every time, or a more polished one, or better words than the ones you used yesterday. David used the same handful of plain requests — hear me, guard me, have mercy, give me joy — over and over across ten verses, and God never once told him to stop repeating himself. Because the God who is "abounding in love to all who call" isn't keeping score of how many times the line rings. He isn't tired of your voice. He's just glad you're still calling. That is, in the end, what makes this psalm feel less like a lesson and more like a hand on your shoulder: you are allowed to need God every single day, in exactly the same way, for as long as this season lasts.

So call again today, in the same plain words, at whatever hour it comes to mind — morning, noon, or the middle of a hard afternoon. It isn't weakness. It's exactly what Marites's children have learned every evening at seven for eleven years: a voice that keeps showing up, on schedule, unhurried, is not a small thing. It is how love proves, one ordinary call at a time, that it never left.

articles.title: The Seventh Item on the List
articles.dek: Proverbs 6 counts off six sins living quietly inside one person — then names a seventh that only exists between people.
articles.quote: God's list of seven doesn't end with the sinner — it ends with everyone standing near him.
articles.illustration: Mandela inviting his Robben Island jailers
articles.body:
On May 10, 1994, in the amphitheater of the Union Buildings in Pretoria, Nelson Mandela stood to take the oath as South Africa's first Black president. Below him sat kings, prime ministers, and more heads of state than the country had ever hosted at once. But three faces in that crowd mattered to Mandela more than any of them. They were his former jailers from Robben Island, the prison where he had spent eighteen of his twenty-seven years locked away, breaking rocks in a limestone quarry that would later damage his eyesight for life. Mandela had personally invited them as guests of honor. One, a young warder named Christo Brand, had once been assigned simply to watch Mandela's cell. Over the years an unlikely friendship grew between them, built on smuggled bread, shared newspapers, and small kindnesses that could have cost the guard his job. By the time freedom came, Mandela had every legal and moral right to let old wounds fester into new conflict — an entire country was watching to see whether he would. Instead he sat his former guards among the dignitaries and thanked them, in public, by name. He had the standing to divide a nation further. He chose, instead, to end a cycle.

That choice sits right at the center of a strange little passage tucked into Proverbs 6 — a passage that reads unlike almost anything else in the book. Most of Proverbs offers gentle, general wisdom: "the way of fools seems right to them" (Proverbs 12:15), "a gentle answer turns away wrath" (Proverbs 15:1). But here, the writer stops being gentle and gets specific. He builds a list — the kind of countdown used elsewhere in Proverbs 30 to name things too wonderful or too wicked to leave uncounted — and tells us plainly what God cannot stand.

"There are six things the Lord hates," he writes, "seven that are detestable to him" (Proverbs 6:16). This "six, then seven" pattern is an old Hebrew way of saying: this list is full — and then some. It isn't a tidy set of six equal offenses. It's an overflow. And when you read down the list, you notice something else: it moves through the body, head to toe. Haughty eyes. A lying tongue. Hands that shed innocent blood. A heart that devises wicked schemes. Feet that are quick to rush into evil. Eyes, tongue, hands, heart, feet — an anatomy of sin, cataloged limb by limb, as if God is naming every part of a person capable of doing damage.

Then the list does something unexpected. The sixth item circles back to speech — "a false witness who pours out lies" — and the seventh, the one that tips the count from six into the "detestable" seven, isn't a body part at all.

"...a false witness who pours out lies and a person who stirs up conflict in the community." (Proverbs 6:19, NIV)

Six things live inside a single person — a wandering eye, a careless tongue, restless hands. But the seventh, the one that pushes the number over the edge into "detestable," only exists between people. You cannot stir up conflict alone. It takes a community to sow discord into. Which means the list isn't just cataloging private vices. It's building toward a warning: the sins that start small and stay inside you are serious, but the sin that spreads — that infects a family, a church, a barangay, a workplace — is the one God singles out as the capstone. It's worth noticing that the same weighty word Scripture uses for idols — "detestable" — is what's used here for someone who quietly turns brother against brother.

That's the piece easy to miss. We tend to rank murder as the obvious horror on this list and treat "stirs up conflict" as the mild one, almost an afterthought — the office gossip, the family group chat, the tita who "just wants everyone to know." But the way this proverb is built, sowing discord isn't a lesser cousin of the other six. It's named right alongside hands that shed innocent blood, as something that costs people their lives together, even when no one bleeds. A rumor doesn't leave a body on the ground. But it can leave a family not speaking for a decade, a church split into two congregations, a friendship dead long before either person admits it.

And this is where the good news breaks in, because every single item on this list was aimed, at some point, straight at Jesus. False witnesses lined up to testify against him (Mark 14:56). Hands that had never wronged anyone were the ones nailed to the wood. A whole crowd, stirred into conflict by leaders with haughty eyes and wicked hearts, screamed for his death instead of Barabbas's. Jesus didn't just teach against this list. He absorbed it — every clause of it, in his own body. And "when he suffered, he made no threats" (1 Peter 2:23). He let the discord end with him instead of passing it forward. Paul later put words to exactly what that accomplished: Christ "is our peace, who has made the two groups one and has destroyed the barrier, the dividing wall of hostility" (Ephesians 2:14). The very thing God calls detestable — a person who stirs up conflict — Jesus reversed by becoming a person who absorbs conflict and hands back peace.

That's the model worth carrying into an ordinary week. Most of us will never devise a wicked scheme or shed innocent blood. But nearly all of us have, at some point, been the seventh item — the one who repeated the story that didn't need repeating, who took sides in someone else's argument for the small thrill of being needed, who let a group chat do what a private conversation should have done instead. Filipino life runs on closeness — big families, tight barkadas, everyone's business somehow becoming everyone's business — which is a gift, but it also means a stirred pot spreads fast and burns a lot of people at once. One unkind retelling at a family reunion can outlive the reunion by years. God's list of seven doesn't end with the sinner — it ends with everyone standing near him.

So here's something practical to carry today: think of one relationship right now carrying old, unresolved friction — not because you have to solve it all at once, but because Mandela's move wasn't complicated. He didn't need a grand reconciliation ceremony to start. He just chose, once, to seat an old enemy somewhere near him instead of somewhere far. You can do a smaller version of that this week. Stop repeating a story that only hurts. Send the message you've been avoiding. Sit near someone instead of talking around them. Let one conversation end differently than it started.

Six things live quietly in a single heart. The seventh only dies when someone decides not to pass it on. Be the one who decides that today.
